title: Yemenite kubaneh
subtitle: overnight enriched pull-apart bread baked in a covered pot
excerpt: Kubaneh is a Yemenite Jewish enriched bread traditionally baked in a covered pot overnight for Shabbat morning. The low, slow heat transforms a yeasted dough into deeply golden, layered pull-apart rolls with a rich, tender crumb. Timing and coverage are everything: the pot must stay sealed during baking or the bread dries out.

glossaryTerms.definition: A bread dough containing fat (butter, oil) and often eggs, sugar, and milk in addition to flour, water, and yeast. The additions tenderise the crumb and slow staling.

Folding fat repeatedly into a dough to build up thin, alternating layers. In bread contexts such as kubaneh, butter is spread across a flattened dough and folded like a letter, creating a layered, pull-apart crumb.
The rest of shaped dough before baking, during which yeast produces gas that expands the loaf. The dough is ready when it has increased noticeably in volume and springs back slowly when pressed.

recipe.freezeNotes: Pull apart into individual rolls after baking, cool completely, and freeze for up to 2 months. Warm in a 160°C oven for 10 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: This is designed to bake overnight (8 hours at low heat). Mix and shape in the evening, slide into the oven before midnight.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: conventional oven; covered pot for the entire 8 hours at 110°C
baking.steamMethod: Steam from dough inside sealed pot; no additional steam needed

content.text: Kubaneh is a Yemenite Jewish
enriched dough
bread baked overnight in a sealed pot at very low heat. You get burnished, pull-apart rolls with a tender, layered interior built by
laminating
butter into thin sheets of dough. The pot seal is critical: any gap lets moisture escape and the bread dries out before morning.

attrs.prepNote: softened to room temperature, for laminating
extra, for greasing the pot and tops of rolls

content.text: Method
Mix the dough
Combine the flour, sugar, salt, and dried yeast in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook. Keep the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl until the liquids go in.

Add the beaten eggs and most of the warm water. Mix on a low speed for 2 minutes until no dry flour remains, then increase to medium and mix for a further 8 minutes. The dough should be smooth, slightly tacky, and pull cleanly from the bowl sides. Add the remaining water a tablespoon at a time if the dough feels stiff.
This is an
enriched dough

: the eggs and the butter added during laminating both enrich and slow the dough, which is why the overnight low-heat bake works so well. The sugar feeds the yeast and contributes to the deep golden crust.
Bulk ferment
Shape the dough into a ball, return it to the lightly oiled mixing bowl, and cover with cling film or a damp cloth. Leave at room temperature for 90 minutes, or until roughly doubled in volume.

While the dough bulk ferments, take the 50 g of softened butter out of the refrigerator if it is not already at room temperature. It needs to be spreadable but not melted: if you press a finger into the block, it should leave an indent easily and the butter should hold its shape.
Laminating the dough with butter
In bread baking,
laminating

means spreading fat across a thin sheet of dough and then folding or rolling it to create distinct layers. Each layer of butter separates adjacent sheets of dough during baking, producing a pull-apart texture with visible strata in the crumb. This is not the same as croissant lamination (which uses chilled block butter and repeated folds for hundreds of layers): kubaneh laminating is a simpler, single-pass technique done at room temperature, closer to the butter-rolling used in babka or morning buns.

Once the dough has doubled, turn it onto a clean, lightly floured surface. Divide it into 7 equal pieces using a bench scraper: one slightly larger piece for the centre and six roughly equal pieces for the outside. Each outer piece should weigh about 85-90 g; weigh them on your digital scales for consistency.

Work one piece at a time. Using your hands or a rolling pin, flatten the piece into a thin oval or circle, roughly 20 cm across. You want it thin enough to see light through it if you held it up, but not so thin that it tears.

Using a pastry brush or your fingertips, spread a thin, even layer of the softened butter across the entire surface of the dough sheet, going right to the edges. Use approximately 6-7 g of butter per piece; you have 50 g total for seven pieces.

Roll the sheet up tightly from one long edge into a thin cylinder, then coil the cylinder into a tight spiral, tucking the end underneath. This coiled shape is a single roll. Set it aside on the floured surface and repeat with the remaining pieces.

The key actions at this stage are: thin sheet (so butter distributes evenly across many layers), a tight roll (so the layers stay defined through the bake), and a firm coil tuck (so the spiral does not unwind during proving). If the butter squeezes out as you roll, it is too warm: chill the dough for 10 minutes and try again.
Arrange in the pot and prove

Generously butter the inside of a 24 cm round cast-iron pot or Dutch oven (it must have a tight-fitting lid). Place the larger coil in the centre, then arrange the six smaller coils around it in a ring. They will be touching lightly; leave a small gap between them as they will expand during proving.
Dot the tops of the rolls with tiny knobs of the extra butter: this helps the tops colour evenly and adds richness to the outer surface during the long, slow bake.
Cover the pot with its lid and leave the rolls to
prove
for 60 minutes at room temperature. They are ready when they have puffed noticeably and are touching each other snugly. Do not allow them to overproof to the point of touching the lid.
Overnight bake
Heat the oven to 110°C conventional. Place the covered pot in the oven. Do not open the lid during baking.

Bake for 8 hours. Traditionally this runs from late evening until morning: the bread is ready for breakfast. At 110°C, the low ambient heat cooks the dough gently and evenly while the steam trapped inside the sealed pot keeps the crumb moist throughout.

After 8 hours, remove the pot from the oven. The rolls should be deep amber to mahogany on top and smell of toasted butter. Lift the lid carefully: the steam inside is very hot. Turn the rolls out onto a wire rack. They should come away as a cluster of pull-apart rolls.

Serve warm, pulling the rolls apart at the table. Kubaneh is traditionally served with hard-boiled eggs (also cooked overnight in the oven at the same temperature) and spicy zhug or tomato dip on the side.

attrs.avoid: Avoid any gap between the pot lid and the rim during baking. Steam trapped inside is what keeps the crumb tender over 8 hours. If your pot lid is loose, seal the gap with a strip of foil before putting it in the oven.
Avoid using butter that is too warm. It should be spreadable with a brush but firm enough to hold a shape. If your kitchen is warm, chill the rolled pieces for 10 minutes before coiling.

attrs.problem: Rolls did not colour, crumb is pale and stodgy
attrs.avoid: Avoid opening the oven door during the bake. The colour develops from prolonged low heat and the sugars in the dough; it takes time. If after 8 hours the rolls are very pale, remove the lid and return the pot to a 180°C oven for 10 minutes.

attrs.problem: Layers are not visible in the crumb
attrs.avoid: Avoid spreading butter too thickly or rolling the cylinder too loosely. A loose roll lets the layers merge. Roll firmly, and use no more than 6-7 g of butter per piece.

attrs.problem: Rolls overproofed and touched the lid before going in the oven
attrs.avoid: Avoid leaving the rolls to prove in a warm spot for longer than 60 minutes. If they have already reached the lid before the oven is ready, place the pot in the oven immediately at 110°C even if the preheat is not complete.
